body_markdown:
As LL Cool J once pontificated, “ *Don’t call it a comeback, I’ve been here for years.* ” The message applies to Hip-Hop Icons and vintage mobile audio head units alike. There’s still a loyal following for both, even if mainstream radio stations or automotive electronics manufacturers didn’t care about what’s happening under their collective radars. Thanks to places like automotive forums and eBay auctions, true believers of high-quality vintage audio never left the scene. They’ve not only kept the flame alive, but they’ve ensured that you can enjoy old cars *and* quality audio at the same time.


As of this year, Pioneer felt the need to embrace their audio heritage. But that was the latest splash into the throwback segment, as Blaupunkt saw the writing on the wall back in 2019. In 2021, Alpine brought back their iconic “green chiclet” on a somewhat retro, somewhat modern head unit. Perhaps their success inspired Pioneer to follow suit, and then the rocket-like appreciation of air-cooled Porsches made for a compelling business case for Blaupunkt to update their classic cassette deck. Ironically, none of these modern units actually have a cassette player, but they combine stylistic elements of the past with the technology that modern audiophiles demand.


Blaupunkt Bremen SQR 46 DAB


Blaupunkt


Alpine HDS-7909


Alpine


Pioneer SXT-C10PS


Pioneer


Bluetooth, HD radio, USB inputs, and even customizable colors for the backlights are par for the course in these radios. Both the Blaupunkt (Bremen SQR 46 DAB) and the Pioneer (SXT-C10PS) look like the tape decks of their respective brands’ past offerings, but the “tape door” masks inputs for modern-day audio sources. USB and AUX plugs are behind the tape door of the Pioneer, but the Blaupunkt goes a step further with an SD card input in the same area. The Alpine doesn’t even pretend to care about vintage media inputs, opting for a purely digital experience behind its iconic button-laden face. (It also seems to be hard to come by; perhaps it was never a sales success in North America.)


To some extent, these new takes on vintage audio hardware are a “what you see is what you get” affair. If you’re a 911 fan, you may well gravitate to a German Blaupunkt the same way you prefer a Porsche 911 SC over a Corvette C4. Blaupunkts have been factory-fitted in countless European vehicles for decades, giving them an edge for purists and audiophiles alike. They have other retro radios, and the[Blaupunkt Frankfurt](https://www.blaupunkt.com/product/frankfurt-stereo) looks ideal for many 50-plus-year-old classics.


Since our eardrums are all tuned a little differently, I suggest you compare and contrast the specifications of the Blaupunkt ([here](https://www.blaupunkt.com/product/bremen-sqr-46-dab) ) and the Pioneer ([here](https://usa.pioneer/collections/heritage/products/sxt-c10ps) ) to see which one does a better job for your needs. I have yet to experience the Pioneer, but I have a feeling the above video hits the nail on the head: Pioneers—and all Japanese audio companies of the era—were generally known for superior sound quality, and it appears to remain true in 2026.


But there really is no wrong answer, especially if you run RCA cables to a separate amplifier, which you can tune to your tastes. The Blaupunkt looks perfect in any European vehicle, while the Pioneer will certainly appeal to American and Japanese cars that need to look like they were Kings of the parking lot in 1987.


eBay


Then again, king is a relative term: It’s such a shame that Alpine isn’t joining in on the fun, as I would drain my bank account for a derivation of the iconic 7909 with a copper (yes, really) chassis. It was, and might still be,[the best head unit ever made](https://www.theautochannel.com/news/2009/02/10/418388.html) . And if high watermarks like Alpine’s 7909 ensure today’s retro radios still cannot scratch your particular itch, *well* , have I got good news: You can learn from my endeavors in that regard.


There are plenty of serviced and reconditioned radios on places like eBay. Back in 2022, I came to terms with the dead[Eclipse Commander navigation radio](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/when-a-trip-down-memory-lane-ends-at-the-scrapyard/#:~:text=I%20really%20tried,least%20in%20theory.) in my 1979 Continental Mark V Collector’s Series. So I did a Google image search to find something worthy of the space it vacated.


Mark V’s love 1990s Silver Faced Pioneers


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


1972 Mark IV, with graphic equalization


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


I soon realized the[Pioneer Premier DEH-P800PRS](https://www.crutchfield.com/S-sQNKkukS1Yj/p_130P800PRS/Pioneer-Premier-DEH-P800PRS.html) would offer the features and the decadent styling worthy of my car’s cabin, as I only had a vague recollection of this stereo until Google helped me secure its full name. I knew this stereo was the right fit, and it paired well with my audio intentions of its older brother, a 1972 Mark IV with a surprisingly stout, shaft-style stereo system.


My Mark VIII’s Kenwood stack.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


My Cougar’s matching Pioneer stack.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


Project Valentino’s McIntosh CD player and Alpine EQ


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


The stack of Kenwood (CD player, pre-amp graphic equalizer) goodness in my Mark VIII was purchased from my brother and has only needed one service from a local electronics repair shop in my 25+ years of ownership. The CD player’s laser (unobtainium, naturally) eventually died, but I found another head unit on eBay for less than the cost of the repair. The Cougar and[Project Valentino](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/project-valentino/) have audio equipment that both met the space constraints of their respective dashboards and my aesthetic and tonality tastes, found with the help of Google and eBay.


So fear not if this new wave of retro-inspired audio equipment doesn’t entirely scratch your itch. The Internet likely has everything you need, but be aware that vintage audio pricing has gone through the roof: all of the items I purchased 5+ years ago have multiplied in value. It’s also crucial to have an electronics repair shop in your back pocket, as old electronics can and will fail on a long enough timeline in your dashboard.


Be it off-the-shelf reboots from famous manufacturers or creating something properly vintage with the likes of eBay and electronics repair shops in your arsenal, an elevated audio experience isn’t hard to achieve in an older car. You can have a look that takes you back with sound quality that pushes you upward.
